# Integrating agency and resource dependency theories: the moderating efect of board size on the relationship between dividends and frm value in Malaysia
Mohd Ashari Bakri1[*](http://orcid.org/0000-0002-3698-0931) , Nurjeehan Ayub1 and Hanefa Muchlis Gazali1
## **Abstract**
**Purpose** This paper aims to examine the moderating efects of board size on the relationship between dividends and frm value in Malaysian settings. The theoretical foundations of this research were the integration between agency and resources dependency theories.
**Design/methodology/approach** Panel data are extracted from DataStream and the annual report for the period of 2012 to 2021, and pooled OLS, random efects, and fxed efects analyses were employed to examine the relationship. Breusch–Pagan Lagrange multiplier (LM) test and the Hausman test used to determine the most appropriate between these three analyses (OLS, random efects, and fxed efects). The results are valid even after calculating the robust standard error to mitigate the potential heteroskedasticity and serial correlation.
**Findings** The empirical results show that board size positively moderates the relationship between dividends and frm value in all the models tested. The results indicate that a larger board of size can minimize the agency problem (agency theory) because a larger board size can more efectively monitor and control management's opportunistic behavior due to more set of skilled and talented individuals included in the boardroom (resources dependency theory). Additionally, efective monitoring can also lead to the increase in dividend payout to maintain a good reputation among investors and simultaneously increase frm value.
**Practical implication** This study contributes to helping the regulators and industry players in Malaysia to improve existing guidelines for determining dividend and board size to increase frm value. The fndings may also provide inputs to the policymakers in recommending the optimum dividend and board size that resulting an increase in valuation.
**Originality/value** By incorporating agency and resources dependency theory, authors investigate the moderating efect of board size on dividend and frm value relationships in Malaysian markets.
**Keywords** Dividend, Firm value, Board size, Agency theory, Resources dependency
*Correspondence: Mohd Ashari Bakri mohd.ashari@ums.edu.my

Te dividend puzzles concept remains one of the most debated topics over the past several decades to date. Te concept of the dividend puzzle emerged when the infuential works of Gordon [[17]](#page-9-0), Lintner [[31,](#page-9-1) [32]](#page-9-2), and Miller and Modigliani [[34]](#page-9-3) proposed some concepts related to dividends. On the other hand, Lintner introduced an economic formula to determine the optimal dividend policy of a frm. Perhaps one of the most infuential papers that led to the controversy over the dividend puzzle was presented by Miller and Modigliani [[34](#page-9-3)]. Te infuential work of Miller and Modigliani [[34](#page-9-3)] was the catalyst for the development of dividend irrelevance theory. Te theory states that in a perfect capital market, the dividend is not related to the value of the frm and there is no confict between shareholders and managers (no agency costs). Te theory also assumes that all investors have equal access to all information (no information asymmetry) and that no costs are incurred when selling and buying shares (no trading frictions). However, this assumption falls short due to the existence of agency costs, information asymmetry, and trading costs. For example, frictions exist as part of the trading process and frictions such as information asymmetry and agency costs infuence the amount and timing of the dividend and afect the value of the frm [[26]](#page-9-4). Te opposite argument posited dividend is related to the value of the frm, and this is known as the dividend relevance theory.
Te relevance theory of dividends suggests that an increase in dividends positively infuences a frm position in the stock market and vice versa. Te pioneers of dividend relevance theory, Lintner and Gordon [[31]](#page-9-1), posited that shareholders prefer dividends to capital gains. Tis argument suggests that investors are risk averse and prefer to reduce uncertainty causing frms to discount frm earnings at a lower rate and thus all things being equal place better value on frms. However, some other researchers later argue that it should not really matter whether a company pays a dividend or not. As a result, the motive of paying dividends to increase frm value remains controversial to this day. One of the earliest theories to support this claim is the dividend signal theory. Te concept of dividend signals is supported by Woolridge (1983), who states that changes or signals about changes in dividends are one of the main drivers of changes in stock prices. Fama and French [[15]](#page-9-5) later documented that dividends can convey information that reinforces a positive relationship between dividends and frm value. Motivated by this inconsistency the study aims to provide an insight into the relationship between dividends and frm value and bridging the gaps by discovering whether board size can moderate the relationship. Additionally, the study is also motivated by real issues namely the increased concern for competitiveness of frms to increase frm value.
In Malaysia, the relationship between dividends and firm value has been studied by academics for
more than a decade. The increase in competitiveness becomes one of the driving factors for the emergence of this topic. In particular, increasing globalization, economic development, emphasis on sustainability, and information technology are becoming driving factors for corporate competitiveness. For instance, the Malaysian economy records an increase of 3.3% in the third quarter of 2023 and an increase of 2.9% in the second quarter of 2023, leading to an overall growth of 3.9% in 2023 [[9](#page-9-6)]. As a result, the increase in firm value becomes a critical factor to be considered by shareholders and investors. To significantly increase firm value, paying out dividends is known to be one of the great strategies.
Te study was motivated not only by the real issue of the need to enhance frm value in Malaysian frms but also by the unclear discovery of the relationship between dividends and frm value in the Malaysian context. Much recent empirical evidence supports a positive relationship between dividends and frm value in Malaysia [[4](#page-9-7)]. Despite ample empirical evidence to support these claims, the signaling theory has been refuted with empirical evidence that dividends are irrelevant to frm value (Chen et al., 2002, Irum et al., 2012). Additionally, Bakri [[5](#page-9-8)] also discovered a negative association between dividends and frm value, where audit quality becomes a moderator for the study. Using dividend yield as a proxy for dividend, dividend and frm value relationship is rather inconsistent compared to the existing empirical evidence in the Malaysian context [[4](#page-9-7)] and relevant theories of dividends. Tis inconsistency contributes to the need for further research into the dividend puzzle.
Our study specifcally posited that this inconsistency may be due to the size of the board, which could potentially strengthen the relationship. Board size's relationship with frm performance is considered to be a fundamental issue in corporate governance [[10](#page-9-9)]. Agency theory describes the board size relationship with corporate performance in two diferent ways. Te frstview, the economics perspective, perceived that the smaller board size increases monitoring and control and thus enhancesoverall corporate fnancial performance [[20]](#page-9-10). However, past empirical evidence neglects to incorporate the resources dependency theory with agency theory to better explain the association between dividends, board size, and frm value. As pointed out, the idea of integrating agency theory with resourcedependency extends the former's gamut. In line with the suggestion, integrate the two theories and explain that the increases in board size also means better monitoring and mitigating the agency cost (agency theory) because a bigger board size improves advisory capacity,
Bakri *et al. Future Business Journal (2024) 10:37 *Page 3 of 10
deliberation, and external relations (resources dependency) and thereby enhance corporate fnancial performance [[40](#page-9-11)].
Empirically, board size is often shown negative association with frm performance in the Malaysia context. As found in many previous studies [[6](#page-9-12), [30,](#page-9-13) [33]](#page-9-14), board size is associated with a negative impact on frm performance. However, many previous studies neglect the concept of agency theory in relation to resources dependency theory in reducing the agency problem as well. For example, increasing the size of the board of directors also means increasing monitoring and control mechanisms providing a larger size of talent and skills, which reduces the agency problem and the likelihood of management misconduct (e.g., tunneling incentives or investing in unprofitable projects).
In addition to the theoretical aspect, we also discuss the empirical aspect or the discovery of this relationship. To get a better insight into the relationship between board size and dividend as well as frm value, the study frst looks at the previous empirical relationship between board size and dividend. Previous empirical studies have found that board size positively infuences dividend payout. For instance, Elmagrhi et al. [[14]](#page-9-15) found a positive relationship between board size and dividend payout among small and medium-sized companies in the UK for the period from 2010 to 2013. Similarly, Khan [[25]](#page-9-16) and García-Meca, E et al. [[16](#page-9-17)] in a recent empirical study found that board size is positively associated with dividends. Te results suggest that not only the strong positive association between board size and dividend was found in much earlier studies, but also in most of the more recent studies. Tis also suggests a strong and consistent positive relationship between board size and dividends.
Second, and fnally, we discuss the empirical evidence for the relationship between board size and frm value. Te empirical evidence for this relationship is quite abundant. For example, Mak and Kusnadi [[33](#page-9-14)] found a negative relationship between board size and frm value in Malaysia and Singapore, suggesting that the larger the board, the lower the frm value. A much earlier empirical study in small companies also found a negative correlation between board size and enterprise value in Finnish companies [[13](#page-9-18)]. A study in Australian companies has also found a strong negative correlation between board size and enterprise value, and the result also shows that this correlation is stronger in small companies [[35]](#page-9-19). A recent empirical study also found a negative relationship between board size and frm value [[6,](#page-9-12) [30]](#page-9-13). Despite the negative relationship between board size and frm value, our studies suggest that the property of board size would
increase frm value in mitigating the agency problem by controlling and monitoring dividend payouts. In other words, the positive efect of board size on ensuring better dividend payout would outweigh the negative efect of board size on frm value.
Te rest of this chapter is as follows: Te next section deals with the literature review, followed by the methodology, the results, the discussion and fnally the conclusion based on the discovery of the results.
## **Literature review and hypothesis development**
Te topic of dividends and frm value is still relevant today because of its signifcant contribution in the feld of corporate fnance. Te dividend decision is of great importance to frms as it indicates their performance and future growth potential [[2](#page-9-20), [43](#page-9-21)]. Leary and Michaely [[28]](#page-9-22) documented that managers place a premium on the stock of a company that pays a stable dividend and that managers behave in such a way that the dividend matters for frm value. While there is ample empirical evidence and theory to support the relevance of dividends to frm value, early theory on the relationship between dividends and frm value established their irrelevance. In general, the dividend and frm value relationship can be divided into two schools of thought. Te frst school of thought was pioneered by the relevance theory of dividend, and this theory posited that dividend poses an impact on frm value. On the contrary, the second school of thought provides the opposite claim where dividend is irrelevance on frm value.
### **Dividend irrelevance theory**
Dividend irrelevance theory is considered to be one of the most remarkable theories in the world of corporate fnance, frst put forward by Nobel Prize winners Miller and Modigliani [[34]](#page-9-3). Te theory assumes that in a perfect capital market, the dividend payout is not related to the value of the frm. Te theory also assumes that in an ideal business world, there are no conficts between shareholders and managers and that investors have equal access to all information. Furthermore, according to this theory, there are no costs for buying and selling shares and no diference is seen between the tax rates for dividends and capital gains. Furthermore, the theory suggests that the dividend policy follows the investment decision made, which then becomes the residual dividend policy and thus results in the dividend having no impact on the value of the frm.
### **Dividend relevance theory**
In contrast to the theory of dividend irrelevance, the theory of dividend relevance comprises several theories that
Bakri *et al. Future Business Journal (2024) 10:37 *Page 4 of 10
underpin the relevance of dividends for frm value. In this study, we discuss the most important and infuential theories of dividend relevance.
#### *Bird in hand theory*
Tis theory states that in a world of economic uncertainty, investors prefer dividends (i.e., a bird in the hand) and capital gains (i.e., two in the hand). Te latter may be correlated with the future of the company, which is much riskier than the current dividend. Terefore, they are willing to pay a higher price for companies with dividend payments, which leads to a higher company value [[18,](#page-9-23)[ 45](#page-9-24)].
#### *Signaling theory*
In general, information asymmetry arises when one party has more information than another. In the context of corporate governance, a company is likely to have more information about current and future company performance than an outsider. Terefore, managers can use the dividend as a tool to give signals to the fnancial market about current and future company growth [[23]](#page-9-25). In addition, Lintner [[31]](#page-9-1) has highlighted managers' concerns about the signal of the company's earnings distribution over time. Accordingly, Bhattacharya's [[7]](#page-9-26) proposition describes how the dividend serves as a function of the frm's fnancial health, which is indicated by the dividend payout refecting future frm performance. Teoretically, a higher dividend signals a higher valuation of the frm.
#### *Agency theory and free cash fow hypothesis*
In addition, agency theory and free cash fow hypothesis are also used to prove the relevance of dividends to frm value. Agency theory suggests that the interests of shareholders and managers are not the same, and thus, dividends can act as a control mechanism to better control cash fow (monitor). Additionally, the free cash fow hypothesis implies that dividends are paid to shareholders to prevent the manager from misusing capital. Jensen [[21]](#page-9-27) argues that free cash fow at the managerial level may lead to investment in unproftable investment opportunities. Terefore, investors prefer a frm that minimizes agency costs by paying higher dividends. As a result, investors invest more in such a frm than in a frm that pays little or no dividends [[42]](#page-9-28).
#### *Empirical evidence on dividend relevance*
Te importance of the dividend for the value of the company is not only discussed in the theories but also empirically examined. Empirical evidence shows a positive relationship between dividends and frm value, but it is controversial how dividends afect frm value. For example, Fama and French [[15](#page-9-5)] found a positive relationship
between dividends and frm value and argued that this is because dividends pick up information about the frm's future business prospects. Pinkowitz et al. [[42](#page-9-28)], on the other hand, argue that investors value a frm that pays dividends better because they appreciate the frm's eforts to mitigate the agency problem (better corporate governance). A mixed argument has been put forward by Baker and Wugler (2004) who claim that the relationship between dividends and frm value depends on the premium that could lead to a positive or negative association.
Up to a decade later, the inconsistency between dividends and enterprise value persists. For example, Dang et al. [[11](#page-9-29)] and Bakri [[5]](#page-9-8) discover a positive relationship between dividend and frm value in Vietnam and Malaysia, respectively. However, Bakri [[4]](#page-9-7) and Sondakh [[44](#page-9-30)] also found a negative relationship between dividends and frm value. For example, Bakri [[4](#page-9-7)] demonstrated that dividends have a negative impact on frm value when dividend yield is used as a proxy for dividends. In terms of distributable net income, the dividend policy shows how successful the company is in increasing shareholder wealth [[19](#page-9-31)]. In terms of a company's fnancial performance, dividend policy is also a factor that determines the success of the frm. Previous research has examined the impact of the dividend payout ratio on frm value in detail [[1]](#page-9-32) and found that the dividend payout ratio has a positive efect on share price, which refects the value of the frm.
However, Dennis and Smith [[12](#page-9-33)] claim that dividend policy has a detrimental efect on frm value. Setting an artifcial dividend can lower the value of the company as it diverts capital from investment to consumption of luxury goods. Dennis and Smith [[12](#page-9-33)] also found in a separate analysis that dividend policy has no impact on frm value. Te inconsistency of the relationship between dividends and frm value suggests that a possible moderating factor could infuence this relationship. We therefore suspect that board size may contribute to this inconsistency and could be an important moderating factor. Past empirical evidence has shown that board size positively afects dividends [[14,](#page-9-15) [16,](#page-9-17) [25]](#page-9-16) and, on the contrary, negatively afects frm value [[6](#page-9-12), [13,](#page-9-18) [30](#page-9-13), [33](#page-9-14), [35]](#page-9-19). After considering the empirical aspect of the relationship, the next section discusses and develops the hypothesis based on the theoretical aspect supported by the empirical aspects discussed in this section.
#### **Agency theory, dividend and frm value**
Agency theory was originally developed by Jensen and Meckling in 1976 [[22](#page-9-34)]. Tis theory states that the governance mechanism of a frm or organization is based on the conficts of interest between the company owner
Bakri *et al. Future Business Journal (2024) 10:37 *Page 5 of 10
(shareholder), the manager and the provider of capital in the form of outside capital. According to this theory, the agency problem is something inevitable and the only way to control it is through the use of regulation, instruments, or mechanisms. One of the most popular instruments used or proposed by scholars to potentially mitigate the agency problem is the dividend. Tis idea is supported by the free cash fow hypothesis developed by Jensen in 1986, which states that dividends are paid to shareholders to prevent the manager from investing in unproftable projects and, in the worst case, in his own personal interest (tunneling incentives). Based on this theory, we have thus established that dividends should reduce the agency problem.
#### **Agency theory, board size and frm value**
When it comes to the relationship between board size and frm performance, agency theory also plays an essential role in explaining the basis of this relationship. Agency theory posits that having a larger board grants efcient monitoring by mitigating the CEO denomination inside the board and simultaneously protecting the interest of the shareholder [[3]](#page-9-35). Additionally, the improved monitoring would then lead to uncertainty avoidance, as suggested by Li and Harrison [[29]](#page-9-36), and the reduction in agency costs would eventually lead to better frm performance [[24](#page-9-37)]. However, substantial amount of empirical studies on the relationship between board size and frm performance argues against the agency cost theory. For example, Mak and Kusnadi [[33](#page-9-14)] discover a negative relationship between board size and frm performance in Malaysia and Singapore. Liao et al. [[30]](#page-9-13) and Ben and Chouaibi [[6]](#page-9-12) also fnd a negative relationship between board size and frm performance. Te result of this empirical evidence points to the stewardship theory. Stewardship theory states that a manager left to his own devices acts as a steward of the assets he controls [[24]](#page-9-37).
However, despite the empirical results pointing more to the stewardship theory than to the agency cost theory, we believe that agency costs and resources dependency theories play a more important role when it comes to the relationship between dividends and frm value, at least in the Malaysian context. Tis is because a larger board ensures better control and monitoring of dividend payments to shareholders. Also, a larger board can have more diversity in the board background, e.g., more professionals from diferent felds, who in turn make better decisions for overall performance without compromising the minority (provide dividend payout). In other words, agency theory would potentially outweigh stewardship theory in the relationship between dividend and frm value when board size acts as a moderator.
## **Resources dependency theory, board size and frm value**
Resources dependency theory was introduced by Pfeffer in Salancik in 1978 [[41]](#page-9-38). Te principle of the theory is that an organization such as a frm or proft-oriented organization required to engage with other actors and organizations within its environment to acquire the resources. Concerning board size and frm performance, resource dependency theory suggests that board size is considered to be a bank of resources [[3]](#page-9-35). Tis is because the board size provides the necessary resources, skills, knowledge, and expertise to invest in innovative projects (Chen, 2012). Based on the argument in Sects. ["Agency ](#page-3-0) [theory, dividend and frm value,](#page-3-0)" ["Agency theory, board ](#page-4-0) [size and frm value,](#page-4-0)" and ["Resources dependency theory, ](#page-4-1) [board size and frm value,"](#page-4-1) we thus hypothesize that:
*Hypothesis 1* Board size moderates the relationship between dividend and frm value in Malaysia.
Te study thus aims to unravel this mystery by examining the relationship between these variables, with board size included as a moderator. ## **Methodology**
### **Empirical model**
Te following model specifcation used to examine the moderating efect of board size on dividend and frm value relationship:
$$ \text{Tobin's } Q_{i,t} = \alpha + \beta_1 DPS_{i,t} + \beta_2 \text{Board size}_{i,t} \\ + \beta_3 DPS \cdot \text{Board}_{i,t} + \beta_4 \log(\text{size})_{i,t} \\ + \beta_5 TLTA_{i,t} + \beta_6 \text{Blockholder}_{i,t} \\ + \beta_7 \text{Cash holding}_{i,t} + \varepsilon_t \tag{1} $$
Tobin's q is the frm value, DPS is the dividend per share, board size is the total number of board members in the frm, DPS*board is the interaction term between DPS, and board size used as moderator. In addition to moderator variables, we also add control variables that

Tese variables include TLTA, representing total liabilities relative to total assets, blockholder, representing the percentage of strategic ownership of 5% or more, cash holdings, representing cash and cash equivalents divided by total assets, and εt is the error term. Te sources of the data collected are from DataStream and annual report, the range period is between 2012 to 2021. Te process of collecting data through various fltering processes, for instance, we exclude banks and fnancial sectors in the sample due to this sector being heavily regulated (Dewasiri et al., 2016). Additionally, all individual data were winsorized at 1 and 99 percent percentile to mitigate the potential outlier. We used Stata, specifcally version 17.0, to perform the analysis.

As can be seen, the interaction term "DPS*board size" correlates positively with frm value, which is represented by Tobin's Q. Table [3](#page-6-0) presents a main analysis of the study. Te study uses pooled ordinary least squares (OLSs), random efects (REs), and fxed efects (FEs) for the period from 2012 to 2021. Te study uses a two-stage analysis to determine the most appropriate model for the study. First, we conduct the Breusch–Pagan LM test to determine which model is a better ft between OLS and RE. Te results of the Breusch–Pagan LM test are less than 0.05, indicating that the random efect is a better ft. In the next phase, we used the Hausman test to determine which of RE and FE is more appropriate. Te results of the Hausman test are less than 0.05, indicating that FE is more appropriate. However, for comparison purposes, we still show all the results (pooled OLS, RE and FE) as shown in Table [3.](#page-6-0)
Panel A and B in Table[ 3](#page-6-0) show the results of the pooled OLS and the random efect. Dividend has a signifcant and positive relationship with frm value with a coefcient of 3.1194 and 2.3900, signifcant at the one percent
level. Board size also shows a signifcant and positive relationship with frm value at the one percent level in both pooled OLS and random efect analysis (coefcient 0.0297 and 0.0497). Te interaction terms DPS*board size shows a positive relationship with frm value at the one percent level (0.1654 and 0.1312 coefcient) in both the pooled OLS analysis and the random efects analysis, suggesting that board size signifcantly moderates the relationship between dividend and frm value. Te control variables used in this study are diferently related to dividend. For example, frm size has a negative and signifcant relationship with dividend (−0.1836 and –0.3186 coefcient) at the one percent level in both the pooled OLS analysis and the random efect analysis. In contrast, leverage (TLTA) and cash holding have a positive and signifcant relationship with frm value with coefcients of 1.3941 and 1.5102, respectively, at one percent signifcant level in the pooled OLS. ## **Discussion**
Although a considerable number of studies have examined the relationship between dividends and frm value, the existing evidence remains inconclusive due to inconsistency of results and theory suggesting a contradictory relationship. Terefore, we re-examine the relationship between dividend and frm value by adding board size as a moderator and re-examine on whether the outcome supports the proposed integrated theories of agency and resources dependency.
In the frst part of the analysis, we used pooled OLS, random efects, and fxed efects to identify the role of board size as a moderator between dividends and frm value. In Table [3,](#page-6-0) Panel A, B and C, we fnd a strong relationship between dividend and frm value and a strong positive moderating efect of board size on the relationship between dividend and frm value. Te results are consistent with the earlier fndings of Bakri [[4]](#page-9-7), Dang et al. [[11]](#page-9-29), Fama and French [[15](#page-9-5)]. Te results suggest that frms that pay higher dividends are likely to have better frm valuation and that board size has a signifcant impact on dividend payout, thus contributing to better frm valuation. A notable discovery of the study, based on agency theory, highlights the very important key aspect of board size on the relationship between dividend and frm value. Te discovery suggests that a larger board is more efective in controlling and monitoring opportunistic behavior (agency cost) by management. Since a larger board is associated with more expertise and experience (resources dependency), it can mitigate the agency problem while improving frm performance, including dividend payout [[36–](#page-9-41)[38]](#page-9-42). In the second part of the analysis, we also used pooled OLS, random efects, and fxed efects, but with robust standard error to mitigate potential heteroskedasticity and serial correlation. Te result remains consistent as shown in Table [3.](#page-6-0) Table [4](#page-7-0) also suggests that board size positively afects the relationship between dividend and frm value after addressing the potential concerns of heteroskedasticity and serial correlation. Tis also suggests that the monitoring and control efect of board members increases expertise and experience as the number of members increases, thereby reducing the likelihood of managerial misconduct (i.e., tunneling incentives). Te results of the study once again are consistent with the argument of Ntim [[36]](#page-9-41), Ntim et al. [[37](#page-9-43)] and Ntim et al. [[38]](#page-9-42) that board size could reduce the agency problem and improve dividend payout while increasing frm performance. Te result of the analysis also implies that agency and resource dependency integration can be used to explain this empirical result.
## **Conclusions**
Tis paper examines the moderating efect of board size on the relationship between dividend and frm value using a sample of the Malaysian market for the period 2012 to 2021 by integrating an explanation from agency and resource dependency theories. Our study contributes to the literature in several ways. First, despite numerous empirical studies examining the impact of dividend on frm value, previous studies have neglected the role of board size as a moderator and lack empirical explanation and integration between agency and resources dependency theories aspect to provide more insight into this dividend puzzle, especially in the context of Malaysian markets. Although previous empirical studies have found that board size has a negative impact on frm value, previous empirical studies have neglected the fact that larger board size is associated with more expertise and experience (resources dependency) to infuence the direct negative relationship. Tis can mitigate the agency problem and increase dividend payout, which simultaneously increases frm value. Second, our discovery ofers a number of implications for shareholders, policymakers, and regulators in other countries, particularly those with relatively similar governance environments. Te results suggest that while board size can have a negative impact on frm value, as has been found in many previous studies, regulators, policymakers, and especially shareholders should not only be concerned with the direct negative impact, as board size also serves as a control and monitoring mechanism, especially in providing
better dividend payout, which in turn leads to better frm valuation.
Our study, like all previous studies, is subject to some limitations. First, the data focused on the Malaysian market, so the results may not be generalizable to other regions, especially countries with a diferent governance environment. Future studies could test the impact of board size as a moderator with signifcant diferences in governance environment. Second, the study tested only one moderator, which may not cover the entire mystery of the dividend puzzle. We therefore strongly recommend that future studies also examine other moderators that potentially have a strong relationship with dividends and frm value simultaneously. Furthermore, and in conclusion, the data used in this study focus on secondary data analysis. Future studies should engage in qualitative analysis through face-to-face interviews to gain a better understanding of how board size can actually contribute to mitigating agency problems while increasing dividend payout and frm value.
